**System Overview**  
The model describes a very simple message‑passing system that consists of a single producer (the *sender*) and a single consumer (the *receiver*) that communicate through an abstract channel.  
The channel can hold any number of pending messages, but every message must be one of a fixed, finite collection of identifiers – the eleven distinct values **v0** through **v10**.  
The system never creates duplicate copies of the same identifier; a value can be present at most once in the whole system at any time.

**State Variables**  

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **Pending** | The set of message identifiers that have been placed on the channel by the sender but have not yet been taken by the receiver. |
| **Delivered** | The set of message identifiers that have already been taken from the channel by the receiver. |

Both sets are initially empty, meaning that the channel starts with no messages and the receiver has not received anything.

**Initial State**  
At the start of execution the **Pending** set is empty and the **Delivered** set is empty.

**Actions (State Transitions)**  

1. **Send** – The sender may introduce a new message: it picks any identifier from the fixed collection that is not already present in **Pending** or **Delivered**, and adds it to **Pending**. This models putting a fresh message onto the channel. The action is only allowed while the total number of distinct identifiers already in the system (the size of **Pending** ∪ **Delivered**) is strictly less than the size of the fixed collection, guaranteeing that a new distinct identifier is always available.

2. **Receive** – The receiver may take a message that is currently pending: it selects an identifier that belongs to **Pending**, removes it from **Pending**, and adds it to **Delivered**. This models successful delivery of a message to the consumer.

3. **Drop (optional)** – The model permits the channel to lose a pending message without delivering it, but only under the condition that the overall cardinality constraint (the total number of distinct identifiers in **Pending** ∪ **Delivered**) remains satisfied. In practice this means a message can be removed from **Pending** only when doing so does not allow the system to exceed the limit imposed by the fixed collection of identifiers. The “NoFullDrop” part of the name indicates that the system never drops *all* pending messages at once; at least one pending message must remain unless the set of pending messages is already empty.

All three actions are nondeterministic: at any step the environment may choose any of the enabled actions, and for **Send** and **Receive** it may choose any admissible identifier.

**Invariant (Safety Condition)**  
The invariant maintained by the model captures two essential safety guarantees:

* **No Spurious Reception** – Every identifier that appears in **Delivered** must have been placed into **Pending** earlier. In other words, the set of delivered messages is always a subset of the set of messages that have ever been sent.

* **No Duplication / Cardinality Bound** – The two sets are always disjoint and together contain at most eleven identifiers, i.e., the total number of distinct messages that exist in the system never exceeds the size of the fixed collection **v0 … v10**. Consequently, a particular identifier can never be present in both **Pending** and **Delivered** at the same time, and it can never appear more than once overall.

These conditions together guarantee that the channel never invents new messages, never loses the knowledge that a sent message existed (unless it is explicitly dropped), and never exceeds its logical capacity.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At all times, every message that has been received was previously sent, the sets of pending and received messages are always disjoint, and the total number of distinct messages present in the system never exceeds the eleven predefined values. This ensures that no spurious or duplicated messages can appear and that the system respects its fixed capacity.

**System Overview**

The model describes a tiny thread‑pool system that handles a fixed collection of work items.  
The environment consists of three logical threads:

* **Two worker threads** – identified as *w1* and *w2*.  
* **One remote (client) thread** – identified as *r3*.

The pool is configured with **five distinct work items**.  The remote thread can add (enqueue) items to a shared work queue, while the two workers repeatedly take items from that queue, execute them, and then become available again.  Workers may also go to sleep when there is no work and be awakened when new work arrives.

---

### State Variables (what the model keeps track of)

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **Items** | The immutable set of the five work items that the system knows about. |
| **Queue** | An ordered list (or multiset) of items that have been enqueued by the remote thread but have not yet been started by a worker. |
| **Processed** | The set of items that have already completed execution by a worker. |
| **ThreadState[ t ]** (for each thread *t* ∈ {w1, w2, r3}) | The current status of the thread.  Possible statuses are **Idle** (ready to act), **Busy** (currently executing an item), **Sleeping** (blocked waiting for work), and **Terminated** (not used in this model). |
| **CurrentItem[ t ]** (for each worker thread) | The specific work item that a busy worker is currently executing; undefined when the worker is idle or sleeping. |

All variables are always kept consistent: an item can appear **either** in the Queue **or** in Processed, never in both places, and never outside both collections.

---

### Actions (how the system evolves)

1. **Enqueue (performed by the remote thread r3)**  
   *Precondition*: There exists at least one item that is neither in the Queue nor already Processed.  
   *Effect*: The remote thread selects one such item and appends it to the end of the Queue.  The remote thread then remains idle (it can enqueue again later).  If any worker is currently Sleeping, that worker is immediately transitioned to Idle (i.e., it is “woken up”) so it can later take the newly enqueued work.

2. **StartProcessing (performed by a worker wᵢ)**  
   *Precondition*: The worker’s ThreadState is Idle **and** the Queue is non‑empty.  
   *Effect*: The worker removes the first item from the Queue, records it as its CurrentItem, and changes its ThreadState to Busy.  No other thread can take that same item because it is no longer in the Queue.

3. **FinishProcessing (performed by a worker wᵢ)**  
   *Precondition*: The worker’s ThreadState is Busy.  
   *Effect*: The item stored in CurrentItem is moved into the Processed set, the worker’s CurrentItem becomes undefined, and the worker’s ThreadState changes to Idle.  The item is now considered completely handled.

4. **Sleep (performed by a worker wᵢ)**  
   *Precondition*: The worker’s ThreadState is Idle **and** the Queue is empty.  
   *Effect*: The worker changes its ThreadState to Sleeping, indicating that it will not take any work until it is explicitly woken.

5. **Wakeup (implicit in the Enqueue action)**  
   *Precondition*: At least one worker is Sleeping and a new item is enqueued.  
   *Effect*: The Sleeping worker’s ThreadState is set to Idle, making it eligible to execute the StartProcessing action on the newly added item.

The remote thread never processes items; it only enqueues them.  Workers never enqueue items; they only dequeue, execute, and mark items as processed.

---

### Safety Invariant (what the model guarantees at all times)

The invariant ensures that the system never loses or duplicates work.  Concretely, at any reachable state:

*Every work item is either waiting in the Queue or already in the Processed set, and never in both places at the same time.*  

Equivalently, the union of the Queue and the Processed set is always a subset of the original five items, and the two collections are disjoint.  This guarantees that no item can disappear without being processed and no item can be processed more than once.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At all times, each of the five work items is either still pending in the queue or has already been processed, and no item is simultaneously in both places; therefore, no work item is ever lost or processed twice.

**System Overview**

The model describes a collection of independent logical clocks that each hold an integer “time‑stamp”.  
The clocks are identified by the names *c0* through *c9*; therefore the system contains ten clocks in total.  

Each clock can only store a value in the range **0** up to a fixed upper limit called **BOUND** (the model sets this limit to 10). When a clock reaches the bound and is asked to advance one more step, it wraps around to **0** – the clocks behave like modular counters modulo **BOUND + 1**.

The state of the system is captured by two pieces of data:

1. **Clock values** – a mapping that tells, for every clock name, the integer currently stored in that clock.  
2. **Error measure** – a single integer that records the largest difference (in absolute value) that currently exists between any two clocks. This value is called **ERRMAX** in the configuration (also set to 10). The error measure is recomputed after each clock update.

**Actions (State Transitions)**  

The system evolves by repeatedly performing one of the following nondeterministic actions:

| Action name | What it does | Effect on the error measure |
|-------------|--------------|-----------------------------|
| **Tick(c)** | Choose a clock *c* from the set {c0,…,c9}. Increase its stored integer by one. If the result would be larger than **BOUND**, the value is set to **0** instead (wrap‑around). | After the increment (or wrap), recompute the maximum absolute difference between the updated clock and every other clock; the error measure is updated to that new maximum. |
| **Reset(c)** (optional, present in the original *IntClocks* spec) | Choose a clock *c* and set its value directly to **0**, regardless of its current value. | The error measure is recomputed in the same way as after a Tick. |

Only one clock changes its value in any single step; all other clocks retain their previous values.

**Initialisation**

At the start of the system all clocks are set to **0**, and consequently the error measure is also **0**. This satisfies the bound and error constraints from the outset.

**Safety Goal (Invariant)**  

The model asserts a single invariant that must hold after every possible sequence of actions:

*All clock values stay inside the allowed range (0 … **BOUND**) and the absolute difference between the values of any two clocks never exceeds the configured error limit (**ERRMAX**). In other words, the “error measure” that records the greatest pairwise deviation is always ≤ ERRMAX.*

This invariant is checked continuously by the TLC model checker; any transition that would cause a clock to leave the 0‑to‑BOUND range or would make the pairwise difference larger than **ERRMAX** is prohibited.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At every reachable state, every clock’s integer value is between 0 and the bound (inclusive), and the greatest absolute difference between the values of any two clocks is never greater than the allowed error limit (ERRMAX).

**System Overview**

The model describes a very small concurrent system that consists of a fixed set of worker threads (the constant *Threads*). In the concrete configuration supplied to the model‑checker there are exactly two threads, called *t1* and *t2*. The system maintains two pieces of shared state:

1. **Per‑thread state** – for every thread the model stores a record with two fields:  
   * *pc* (the program counter) which indicates which step of the protocol the thread is currently in, and  
   * *value* (a numeric field) that the thread uses to remember a snapshot of a shared counter.

2. **Shared counter** – a single natural‑number variable that all threads can read and later update.

At the start of execution every thread is in the “Read” phase, its *value* field is zero, and the shared counter is also zero.

---

**Thread Actions**

The system evolves by repeatedly letting any thread perform one of the following actions, or by entering a global “terminating” state once every thread has finished.

| Action | When it can be taken | Effect on the thread’s local state | Effect on the shared counter |
|--------|----------------------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------|
| **Read** | The thread’s *pc* is “Read”. | The thread changes its *pc* to “Inc” and copies the current value of the shared counter into its *value* field. | The shared counter is left unchanged. |
| **Inc** | The thread’s *pc* is “Inc”. | The thread changes its *pc* to “Done”. | The shared counter is updated to the value that the thread stored in its *value* field plus one. |
| **Terminating** | All threads have *pc* equal to “Done”. | No thread state is changed. | The shared counter is left unchanged; the system simply stops making further moves. |

In other words, each thread follows a two‑step protocol:

1. **Read phase** – grab a snapshot of the current counter.  
2. **Increment phase** – write back a new counter value that is exactly one larger than the snapshot it read.

A thread may not skip either step, and it may not perform the increment before it has performed the read. The two steps can be interleaved arbitrarily among the threads: for example, *t1* may read, then *t2* may read, then *t1* may increment, then *t2* may increment, etc.

---

**Safety Goal (Invariant)**

The invariant that the model‑checker verifies is called **NoLostUpdates**. It asserts that **once every thread has reached the “Done” state, the shared counter must equal the total number of threads**. In the concrete instance with two threads, the invariant guarantees that after both threads have completed their two‑step protocol the counter will be exactly 2. The invariant therefore ensures that no increment performed by a thread can be lost or overwritten by another thread’s later actions.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
If all threads have finished their protocol (each is in the “Done” state), then the shared counter’s value equals the number of threads, meaning that every thread’s increment has been correctly applied and no update has been lost.

**System Overview**

The model describes a tiny concurrent system that consists of two independent threads, called **Process a** and **Process b**, that cooperate through two shared integer variables:

* **signal** – a counter that starts at 3 and is used as a simple synchronization primitive.  
* **progress** – a counter that records the amount of work that has been performed. It starts at 0 and the goal of the system is to make it reach 100.

Each thread also has its own private state:

* **exit flag** – a Boolean that is initially *false*. When a thread discovers that *progress* has become exactly 100 it sets its own exit flag to *true* and stops looping.
* **tmp** – a temporary integer used to hold the current value of *progress* while the thread computes a new value.
* **program counter** – an internal marker (not visible to the external world) that indicates which step of the thread’s algorithm is about to be executed.

Both threads run forever until their own exit flag becomes *true*. The specification also allows a “terminating” state where both threads have finished and no variables change any more.

---

### Detailed Behaviour of the Threads  

#### Common Concepts  

* **Loading progress** – the thread copies the current value of the shared *progress* variable into its private *tmp* variable.  
* **Updating progress** – the thread writes a new value into the shared *progress* variable, computed as the private *tmp* plus a constant.  
* **Signalling** – the thread decrements the shared *signal* counter by 1. This represents the thread announcing that it has completed a part of its work.  
* **Waiting for signal** – the thread blocks until the shared *signal* counter has become 0. Only when all expected signal operations have been performed can the thread continue.  

#### Process a (simpler loop)  

1. **Read progress** – store *progress* into its private *tmp*.  
2. **Add 20** – set *progress* to (*tmp* + 20).  
3. **Signal** – decrement *signal* by 1.  
4. **Wait** – stay idle until *signal* reaches 0.  
5. **Read progress again** – store the (now possibly updated) *progress* into *tmp*.  
6. **Check for completion** – if *tmp* equals 100, set its own exit flag to *true*; otherwise loop back to step 1.  

Thus each iteration of Process a contributes **+20** to the shared *progress* and consumes **one** unit of the *signal* counter.

#### Process b (more work per iteration)  

1. **Read progress** – store *progress* into its private *tmp*.  
2. **Add 30** – set *progress* to (*tmp* + 30).  
3. **Signal** – decrement *signal* by 1.  
4. **Read progress again** – store the current *progress* into *tmp* (after the +30).  
5. **Add 50** – set *progress* to (*tmp* + 50).  
6. **Signal** – decrement *signal* by 1 (second signal).  
7. **Wait** – stay idle until *signal* becomes 0.  
8. **Read progress a third time** – store the latest *progress* into *tmp*.  
9. **Check for completion** – if *tmp* equals 100, set its own exit flag to *true*; otherwise loop back to step 1.  

Each iteration of Process b contributes **+30** followed by **+50** (a total of **+80**) to *progress* and consumes **two** units of the *signal* counter.

---

### Synchronisation via *signal*

Both threads use the *signal* counter as a rendez‑vous point:

* Process a issues one signal per iteration.  
* Process b issues two signals per iteration.  

The initial value of *signal* is **3**, which is exactly the number of signals that will be emitted before the first waiting point can be satisfied (one from Process a and two from Process b). After the first waiting point, the two threads continue to emit signals in the same proportion, so the counter always returns to zero before either thread proceeds past its waiting step.

---

### Invariant (Safety Property)

The model includes a single invariant named **SignalNeverGoesBelowZero**. In plain English it guarantees:

> **At every reachable moment during execution, the shared `signal` counter is never negative; its value is always zero or a positive integer.**

This safety condition ensures that the synchronization primitive cannot be over‑consumed, which would indicate a logic error such as a thread waiting for a signal that will never arrive.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** The `signal` counter is always greater than or equal to zero; it never becomes negative.

**System Overview**

The model describes a very small distributed protocol that is executed by a fixed set of participants (called *agents*).  Each agent runs the same two‑step routine in order to contribute one unit to a single shared counter.  The whole system is driven by a global state that is updated atomically by the agents’ actions.

---

### Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **Program counter (pc)** | For every agent a record of which phase of the routine the agent is currently in.  The possible phases are the strings **“Increment”**, **“Update”**, and **“Done”**. |
| **Local state (state)** | For every agent a place to store a snapshot of the shared counter that the agent read.  Initially the entry for each agent is the special value **NULL** (meaning “no value has been read yet”). |
| **Shared counter (counter)** | A single non‑negative integer that all agents collectively increment.  It starts at zero. |

---

### Initialisation

When the system starts:

1. Every agent’s program counter is set to **“Increment”** – the first step of the routine.  
2. Every entry in the local state map is set to **NULL** – no agent has read the counter yet.  
3. The shared counter is set to **0**.

---

### Actions

The protocol consists of three kinds of atomic actions that an individual agent may perform.  Only one agent executes an action at a time.

1. **Transition (internal state change)**  
   An agent may simply change its own program‑counter value from one phase to another, leaving all other variables unchanged.

2. **Load**  
   *Pre‑condition*: the agent is in the **“Increment”** phase.  
   *Effect*: the agent copies the current value of the shared counter into its own entry of the local state.  The shared counter itself does **not** change.

3. **Update**  
   *Pre‑condition*: the agent is in the **“Update”** phase and already has a stored value in its local state (the value it read earlier).  
   *Effect*: the shared counter is replaced by the stored value plus one.  The agent’s local state remains unchanged.

4. **Increment (composite step)**  
   This is the observable step an agent can take, and it has two alternatives:  

   *a. Load branch* – the agent moves from **“Increment”** to **“Update”** and simultaneously performs a **Load**.  
   *b. Update branch* – the agent moves from **“Update”** to **“Done”** and simultaneously performs an **Update**.

   After completing the **Update** branch, the agent has contributed exactly one unit to the shared counter and marks itself as finished.

5. **Terminating**  
   When **all** agents have reached the **“Done”** phase, the system may enter a quiescent mode where no variable is allowed to change any more.  This represents the normal end‑state of the protocol.

The overall system evolution (`Next`) is simply: *pick any agent that is not yet finished and let it execute its Increment step*, or, if everyone is already finished, stay in the terminating state.

---

### Intended Behaviour

Each agent follows the same two‑step pattern:

1. **Read** – capture the current global counter value.  
2. **Write** – write back that captured value increased by one.

Because the actions are atomic and only one agent acts at a time, the writes never interfere with each other.  Consequently, after every agent has performed its write, the global counter should equal the number of agents that have completed the routine.

---

### Safety Property (Invariant)

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
If every agent has finished its routine (i.e., all agents are in the “Done” phase), then the shared counter must equal the total number of agents. In other words, the counter’s value is guaranteed to be exactly the count of agents that have successfully completed the increment operation.

**System Overview**

The model describes a single‑shard instance of the *Unanimous BPaxos* consensus protocol, a variant of the BPaxos protocol that can decide a command in a single “fast” round when a full quorum of acceptors agrees, but can also fall back to the classic two‑phase Paxos flow when the fast round fails.  

The system is composed of four kinds of participants:

| Participant | What it represents | How many instances | Role in the protocol |
|-------------|-------------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| **Dependency‑service replicas** | Nodes that store the *dependency graph* of commands – i.e., for every command they remember which previously‑known commands it conflicts with. | Five (named d1 … d5) | When a client proposes a command, the coordinator contacts a quorum of these replicas to obtain the set of commands that the new command must depend on. |
| **Acceptors** | Classic Paxos acceptors that record the highest round number they have promised and the value (command together with its dependency set) they have accepted. | Five (named p1 … p5) | In the *fast* path they must all accept the same proposal; in the *classic* path any three constitute a quorum. |
| **BPaxos replica (the coordinator/leader)** | The single node that receives client requests, drives the protocol, and ultimately learns the decided command. | One (named n1) | It initiates the dependency‑service phase, proposes the command to acceptors, and performs the classic Paxos fallback if necessary. |
| **Commands** | The client‑issued operations that the system must agree on. The model contains two distinct commands, *a* and *b*. | Two (a, b) | The two commands are declared to *conflict* with each other – meaning they cannot be executed concurrently without ordering. |

All sets are finite, and the model explicitly enumerates the symmetry permutations of each participant type; this lets the model‑checker treat any renaming of replicas as equivalent.

---

### State Variables (conceptual)

| Variable | Meaning (in plain English) |
|----------|----------------------------|
| **DepServiceReplicas** | The five dependency‑service nodes. |
| **DepServiceQuorums** | Any subset of at least three dependency‑service nodes; a quorum is required to obtain a reliable dependency set. |
| **Acceptors** | The five acceptor nodes. |
| **AcceptorFastQuorum** | The *fast* quorum – all five acceptors. A fast decision is possible only when every acceptor accepts the same proposal. |
| **AcceptorClassicQuorum** | Any subset of at least three acceptors; this is the quorum needed for the classic Paxos phase. |
| **BPaxosReplicas** | The single coordinator node. |
| **Commands** | The two possible client commands, *a* and *b*. |
| **Conflicts** | The relation that states *a* conflicts with *b* (and vice‑versa). No command conflicts with itself. |
| **Round** | The numerical identifier of a Paxos round. The model limits the maximum round value to 1, meaning only a single logical round is considered for each command. |
| **CoordinatorOf(I, i)** | A function that maps a command *I* and a logical instance *i* to the coordinator that is responsible for that instance – here it always returns the sole BPaxos replica *n1*. |
| **DependencySet[I]** | (Implicit) The set of commands that the dependency‑service reports as conflicting with command *I* at the moment it is proposed. |
| **AcceptedValue[p]** | (Implicit) For each acceptor *p*, the value (command + its dependency set) that *p* has accepted together with the round number. |
| **ChosenValue[i]** | (Implicit) The command that has been decided for logical instance *i* once a quorum of acceptors has accepted the same value. |

---

### Protocol Actions (described in natural language)

1. **ClientSubmit(command)**  
   *A client sends either command *a* or command *b* to the coordinator (the sole BPaxos replica). The coordinator records the request and starts the processing for the next logical instance.*

2. **GatherDependencies**  
   *The coordinator contacts a quorum of at least three dependency‑service replicas. Each replica returns the set of commands it currently knows that conflict with the newly submitted command. The coordinator merges all replies (taking the union) to obtain the final *dependency set* for the command.*

3. **FastPropose**  
   *Armed with the command and its dependency set, the coordinator sends a *fast proposal* to **all five** acceptors. The proposal carries the round number (0, because the model allows only one round) and the full value (command + dependencies).*  
   *If every acceptor receives the proposal and records it as its accepted value for that round, the command is **instantly chosen** (fast decision).*

4. **FastReject**  
   *If any acceptor cannot accept the fast proposal—because it has already promised a higher round or because it has already accepted a different value for that instance—it replies with a rejection. The fast path therefore fails.*

5. **ClassicPrepare**  
   *When the fast path fails, the coordinator initiates the classic Paxos two‑phase flow. It sends a *prepare* message (containing a new round number) to a **classic quorum** of three acceptors. Each acceptor that has not promised a higher round replies with a *promise* that includes any value it may have already accepted.*

6. **ClassicAccept**  
   *After receiving promises from a classic quorum, the coordinator selects the value with the highest round among the replies (or, if none exist, the original command with its dependency set) and sends an *accept* message with that value to the same quorum. The acceptors record the value as their accepted value for the round.*

7. **Learn**  
   *Once a quorum of acceptors (fast quorum or classic quorum, depending on the path taken) have recorded the same value, the coordinator (and any other learner) can mark the command as **chosen** for that instance. The chosen value is then made visible to the client.*

8. **No‑op / Null handling**  
   *The model also contains a special “NULL” value and a “noop” command that represent the absence of a client request; these are used to keep the state well‑typed when no real command is pending.*

All actions are deterministic with respect to the participants’ local state, and the model assumes reliable, ordered message delivery between the coordinator, the dependency‑service replicas, and the acceptors.

---

### Invariants (what the model checks)

The configuration lists four invariants that must hold in every reachable state:

| Invariant | Intuitive meaning |
|-----------|-------------------|
| **TypeOk** | Every variable always contains a value of the type expected (e.g., each acceptor’s stored value is either a command from the set {a,b} together with a legitimate dependency set, or the special NULL value). |
| **ConsensusConsistency** | No two different commands can be *chosen* for the same logical instance. If a command has been decided, any other command for that instance must be identical. |
| **Nontriviality** | A command is considered *chosen* only if it is one of the real client commands (*a* or *b*); the system never decides the special NULL value as a real decision. |
| **ChosenConflicts** | If two distinct commands are both chosen (perhaps in different instances) and they conflict (a ↔ b), then the dependency information recorded for each must reflect that relationship—i.e., each command’s dependency set must include the other, guaranteeing a consistent ordering. |

---

### SAFETY PROPERTY:
The safety property guaranteed by the invariant set is that **the system never decides two different, conflicting client commands without recording a mutual dependency between them; consequently, for any logical instance at most one command can be chosen, and any chosen command is always a genuine client command that respects the conflict‑ordering constraints.**

**System Overview**

The specification models a tiny concurrent system that consists of two independent threads, called **a** and **b**. Both threads run forever, repeatedly executing a small set of operations that manipulate a handful of shared variables. The threads coordinate their actions through a mutual‑exclusion lock (the *mutex*), a one‑bit *pulse* flag, and an integer resource called the *fortress*. The purpose of the model is to verify that the two threads never occupy the critical section at the same time.

---

### Shared State

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **mutex** | Holds the identifier of the thread that currently owns the lock. It is empty when no thread holds the lock. |
| **mutex_pulse_received** | A Boolean flag that is set to true when the thread that owns the lock sends a *pulse*; it is cleared after the waiting thread observes it. |
| **darkness** | An integer counter that both threads increase on every loop iteration. |
| **evil** | Another integer counter that both threads increase on every loop iteration. |
| **fortress** | An integer that represents a pool of “tokens”. Threads can consume a token (decrement) or add one (increment). |
| **threads_in_critical_section** | The number of threads that are currently inside the critical section. The model uses this to express the mutual‑exclusion invariant. |
| **ok** (used only by thread a) | A temporary Boolean that records whether the first fortress‑wait succeeded. |

All other variables that appear in the low‑level translation (program counters, stacks, temporary locals) are implementation details of the model‑checking machinery and are not part of the functional description.

---

### Primitive Operations

* **Enter mutex** – A thread may acquire the lock only when the lock is free. After the operation the lock records the thread’s identifier.  
* **Exit mutex** – The owning thread releases the lock, returning it to the free state.  
* **Send pulse** – The owning thread sets the *pulse* flag to true; this is used as a notification to another thread that is waiting for the lock.  
* **Wait for pulse** – A thread that has just released the lock suspends execution until it observes that the *pulse* flag has become true, then clears the flag and tries to reacquire the lock. This sequence implements a “hand‑off” protocol between the two threads.  
* **Fortress wait** – A thread may request a token from the fortress. If the request is made with *block = false* the thread checks whether a token is available; if none are available it records failure (sets *ok* to false) but does not block. If *block = true* the thread will wait until a token becomes available, then consume it and record success.  

* **Increment darkness** – Reads the current value of *darkness*, adds one, and writes the result back.  
* **Increment evil** – Same as above but for the *evil* counter.  

* **Enter critical section** – Increments the *threads_in_critical_section* counter.  
* **Leave critical section** – Decrements the same counter.

---

### Thread a – Behaviour

1. **Loop start** – The thread repeats the steps forever.  
2. **Increase counters** – It increments *darkness* and then *evil*.  
3. **Conditional test** – If *darkness* is **not** equal to 2 **and** *evil* is **not** equal to 2, the thread proceeds; otherwise it returns to the top of the loop.  
4. **First fortress wait (non‑blocking)** – The thread attempts to take a token from the fortress without waiting.  
   * If a token is available, the token is consumed and a local flag *ok* becomes true.  
   * If no token is available, *ok* becomes false and the thread aborts the rest of this iteration.  
5. **Second fortress wait (blocking)** – Executed only when the first wait succeeded. The thread now waits until a token is available, consumes it, and keeps *ok* true.  
6. **Additional token consumption** – The thread decrements the fortress once more (removing a third token).  
7. **Lock acquisition** – It acquires the mutex.  
8. **Pulse‑hand‑off** – The thread calls the *wait‑for‑pulse* routine: it releases the lock, waits until it sees the *pulse* flag set by the other thread, clears the flag, and then reacquires the lock.  
9. **Critical section** – While holding the lock, the thread enters the critical section, immediately leaves it, and finally releases the lock.  
10. **Repeat** – The thread goes back to step 1.

---

### Thread b – Behaviour

1. **Loop start** – The thread repeats the steps forever.  
2. **Increase counters** – It increments *darkness* and then *evil*.  
3. **Conditional test** – If *darkness* is **not** equal to 2 **and** *evil* **is** equal to 2, the thread follows the *pulse* path; otherwise it skips to step 5.  
4. **Pulse path**  
   * Acquires the mutex.  
   * Sends a pulse (sets the *pulse* flag).  
   * Releases the mutex.  
   * Enters the critical section, immediately leaves it, and proceeds.  
5. **Fortress release** – Independently of the conditional, the thread increments the *fortress* counter, thereby adding a token to the pool.  
6. **Reset counters** – It resets *darkness* and *evil* to zero.  
7. **Repeat** – The thread goes back to step 1.

---

### Coordination Summary

- Both threads continuously raise the two counters *darkness* and *evil*.  
- Thread a only proceeds when **both** counters are different from 2; thread b only proceeds when *evil* equals 2 while *darkness* is different from 2.  
- The *fortress* token pool is increased by thread b each iteration and consumed by thread a in a two‑step handshake (one optional, one mandatory) plus an extra consumption.  
- The *pulse* flag is used by thread b to notify thread a that it may safely reacquire the lock after having released it.  
- All accesses to the critical section are protected by the *mutex* lock, and the lock hand‑off ensures that the two threads never hold the lock simultaneously.

---

### Safety Property

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** At any moment, the number of threads that are inside the critical section never exceeds one; in other words, the system guarantees mutual exclusion on the critical section.

**System Overview**

The model describes a very small system that consists of three state variables:

* **x** – a collection (set) of exactly 1,001 distinct integer identifiers.  
  When the system starts, these identifiers are chosen uniformly at random from the range **1** through **100 000 000**.

* **y** – a collection (set) of exactly 2 distinct integer identifiers.  
  At initialization these identifiers are chosen uniformly at random from the narrow range **100 000 000** through **100 000 010**.

* **z** – a Boolean flag that represents a simple “enabled” condition.  
  At the moment the system is created the flag is set to **TRUE**.

**Initialization (the start of the system)**  

When the system is first instantiated, it performs the following actions:

1. It draws a random subset of size 1,001 from the large interval 1 … 100 000 000 and stores the result in **x**.  
2. It draws a random subset of size 2 from the small interval 100 000 000 … 100 000 010 and stores the result in **y**.  
3. It sets the Boolean flag **z** to **TRUE**.

**Next‑step behavior (the only transition the model allows)**  

After the initial state, the system can take a single kind of step, called **Next**:

* The two sets **x** and **y** are never altered; they stay exactly as they were at initialization.  
* The Boolean flag **z** is overwritten with the value **FALSE**.  

Because the specification requires that every step be an instance of **Next**, the system will repeatedly execute this same transition: the flag will be set to **FALSE** on the first step and will remain **FALSE** thereafter (the step does not toggle the flag back to **TRUE**).

**Purpose of the model**  

The model is intended to capture the creation of two random subsets together with a simple lifecycle flag that starts true and is permanently cleared after the first transition. It can be used to check whether a property that expects the flag to stay true holds throughout the execution.

---

### SAFETY PROPERTY:
The invariant requires that the Boolean flag **z** must always remain **TRUE**; in other words, at every reachable state of the system the flag is guaranteed to be true.

No messages have been received yet. The sets of correct and faulty processes are chosen nondeterministically subject to the cardinality constraints above. **Process Actions (Step)** A correct process repeatedly executes a *step* that consists of two phases: 1. **Message reception** – the process may atomically add any subset of the messages that have already been sent by correct processes, and optionally any subset of forged “ECHO” messages that Byzantine processes could have generated. This models the asynchronous arrival of messages from the network. 2. **Local transition** – after receiving the new messages, the process evaluates four guarded actions, each corresponding to a clause in the original broadcast algorithm: * **UponV1** – If the process is in state V1 (it has seen the INIT) and has not yet sent an ECHO, it changes its state to SE and adds its own ECHO message to the global *sent* set. * **UponNonFaulty** – If the process is still in V0 or V1, has collected ECHO messages from at least *N − 2·T* different processes, but fewer than *N − T* different processes, it also sends an ECHO (changing to SE). This reflects the rule that a process may forward the broadcast once it has heard from a sufficiently large “non‑faulty” majority but not yet enough to decide. * **UponAcceptNotSentBefore** – If the process has collected ECHO messages from at least *N − T* different processes and has not sent an ECHO before, it both sends an ECHO and moves directly to the accepted state AC. * **UponAcceptSentBefore** – If the process is already in SE (it has sent an ECHO) and now has ECHO messages from at least *N − T* different processes, it moves to the accepted state AC without sending any further messages. Each of these actions updates the process’s control state and possibly augments the global *sent* set; all other variables remain unchanged. **System Evolution** The global transition relation permits any correct process to take a step at any time, while faulty processes are not modeled as taking steps (their behaviour is captured solely through the arbitrary messages that may appear in the *Received* phase). A self‑loop is also allowed so that the system may terminate after no further steps are taken. Weak fairness is imposed on the combination of reception and the guarded actions, ensuring that if a particular guarded action stays enabled forever for a correct process, it will eventually be executed. **Safety Property (Unforgeability)** The invariant of interest is *unforgeability*: if no correct process ever originates an INIT (i.e., every correct process starts in state V0), then no correct process can ever reach the accepted state AC. In other words, a correct process can only accept a broadcast that was genuinely initiated by a correct process; forged messages from Byzantine processes alone cannot cause acceptance. **SAFETY PROPERTY:** If all correct processes start without having received an initial broadcast, then throughout the execution no correct process ever transitions to the accepted state. In plain terms, a broadcast that was never sent by a correct process can never be accepted by any correct process.

**System Overview**

The model describes a simple shared‑resource manager that coordinates a small set of independent components (called *actors*) which consume a limited pool of identical resources. A single timer process periodically refills the pool back to its maximum capacity.

---

### State Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **resources_left** | The current number of unused resources that are still available in the pool. It is initialized to the total capacity of the pool. |
| **resources_needed** | For each actor, the amount of resources that actor still intends to consume. At the start each actor is assigned a demand between one and a configurable maximum. |
| **reserved** | The total amount of resources that have been earmarked for actors that have passed the initial check but have not yet been actually taken from the pool. |
| **pc** (program counter) | For every actor and for the timer, a small state label that records what step the process is currently in. The possible labels are “init”, “working”, and for the timer only “init”. |

---

### Actor Behaviour

1. **CheckConsume (request phase)**  
   - An actor may perform this step only when it is in the “init” state.  
   - The actor looks at the current pool size and the amount already reserved for other actors. If the pool contains enough free resources to satisfy the actor’s whole demand **plus** the resources that are already reserved, the actor reserves exactly the amount it needs.  
   - The reservation counter is increased accordingly and the actor’s state changes to “working”. No actual resources are removed from the pool at this point; they are merely promised.

2. **Consume (actual consumption)**  
   - An actor in the “working” state repeatedly executes this step while it still has resources left to consume.  
   - Each execution removes a single resource from the pool, decrements the actor’s remaining demand by one, and also reduces the reservation counter by one (because the reserved resource is now truly consumed).  
   - The actor stays in the “working” state until its demand reaches zero.

3. **RebootConsumer (reset phase)**  
   - When an actor has finished consuming all of the resources it previously reserved (its demand has reached zero) and it is still in the “working” state, it may reset itself.  
   - The actor picks a new demand value anywhere between one and the maximum allowed per actor.  
   - Its state returns to “init”, ready to start a new request cycle. The pool size and the reservation counter are left unchanged during this reset.

---

### Timer Behaviour

1. **Refill (restocking the pool)**  
   - The timer process, which is always in the “init” state, may at any moment reset the pool.  
   - When it does so, the number of free resources is set back to the full capacity of the pool.  
   - No other variables (actor states, demands, or reservations) are altered by a refill.

---

### Execution Model

- The system evolves by repeatedly selecting one of the enabled actions: any actor may try to request resources, consume one unit, or reset itself; the timer may refill the pool.  
- The specification guarantees that each of these actions will eventually be taken if it remains continuously enabled (weak fairness).  
- The initial configuration starts with the pool fully stocked, no reservations, each actor assigned a random demand between one and the maximum, and all processes in the “init” state.

---

### Safety Property

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** The number of free resources in the pool never becomes negative; the pool size is always greater than or equal to zero. This guarantees that the system never “over‑draw” resources, even when multiple actors reserve and consume concurrently.

**System Overview**

The model describes a simple asynchronous communication system consisting of a *sender*, a *receiver*, and a *channel* that can hold a collection of messages. All possible messages are taken from a fixed catalog of eight identifiers – `v0` through `v7`. The channel is represented as a set, meaning it can contain any subset of those identifiers, but never more than one copy of the same identifier.

**State Variables**

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **Channel** | The current set of messages that have been placed in the channel by the sender and have not yet been taken by the receiver. |
| **Sent** | The cumulative set of all messages that have ever been put into the channel (including those that may already have been removed). |
| **Received** | The cumulative set of all messages that the receiver has taken out of the channel. |

Both *Sent* and *Received* are monotonic: once a message is added to either set it never disappears. The *Channel* set is always exactly the difference between *Sent* and *Received* (i.e., the messages that have been sent but not yet received).

**Actions**

1. **Send**  
   - The sender may, at any step, choose any message from the fixed catalog that is **not already present** in the channel.  
   - The chosen message is added to the *Channel* set, and the same message is also added to the *Sent* set, recording that it has been transmitted.

2. **Receive**  
   - The receiver may, at any step, choose any message that is currently present in the *Channel* set.  
   - The chosen message is removed from the *Channel* set and added to the *Received* set, recording that it has been delivered.

3. **No‑Full‑Drop Constraint**  
   - The model does **not** contain any action that can discard the whole content of the channel in a single step.  
   - The only way messages leave the channel is through the *Receive* action, which removes exactly one message at a time. Consequently, the channel can become empty only after a series of individual receives, never by a “drop‑all” operation.

**Initial State**

At the start of the system, all three sets are empty: no messages have been sent, none have been received, and the channel holds no messages.

**Safety Property (Invariant)**

The invariant guarantees three essential safety conditions throughout every possible execution:

1. **Membership** – Every message that appears in the channel is one of the eight predefined identifiers (`v0` … `v7`).  
2. **No Duplicates** – Because the channel is a set, it never contains the same identifier more than once.  
3. **Consistent Accounting** – At any moment the channel’s content is precisely the set of messages that have been sent but not yet received; formally, *Channel* = *Sent* − *Received*.

These conditions together ensure that the system never loses or corrupts a message, never creates a phantom message, and never drops the entire backlog in a single step.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system always maintains that the channel contains only distinct messages drawn from the predefined catalog, and that the channel’s content exactly equals the set of messages that have been sent minus those that have already been received. This invariant guarantees that no message is lost, duplicated, or introduced spuriously, and that the channel can only become empty through successive individual receives, never by an instantaneous full‑drop operation.

**System Overview**

The specification models the classic *dining philosophers* problem for a configurable number of philosophers sitting around a circular table.  

- **Philosophers**: The system contains a set of philosophers numbered from 1 up to *NumPhilosophers*. The constant `NumPhilosophers` must be a positive integer.  

- **Forks**: There is exactly one fork positioned between each pair of adjacent philosophers, so the number of forks equals the number of philosophers. Forks are also numbered from 1 to *NumPhilosophers*. Fork k is physically to the right of philosopher k and to the left of philosopher k + 1 (with wrap‑around: the right fork of the last philosopher is fork 1).  

- **State Variables**  
  1. **Program Counter (`pc`)** – a map that records, for each philosopher, which step of the algorithm it is currently executing. The possible steps are:  
     - *GetFirstFork* – the philosopher is trying to pick up the first fork.  
     - *GetSecondFork* – the philosopher has already taken the first fork and now tries to take the second.  
     - *Eat* – the philosopher holds both forks and is eating.  
     - *ReleaseLeftFork* – the philosopher is about to put down the fork on its left side.  
     - *ReleaseRightFork* – the philosopher is about to put down the fork on its right side.  
  2. **Fork Ownership (`forks`)** – a map that records, for each fork, which philosopher (if any) currently holds it. A special value `NULL` indicates that the fork is free.  

**Initialisation**

When the system starts, every philosopher’s program counter is set to *GetFirstFork* and all forks are free (`NULL`).  

**Behaviour (Actions)**  

The system evolves by repeatedly performing one of the following actions, chosen nondeterministically for any philosopher that satisfies the required pre‑conditions.

1. **GetFirstFork**  
   - A philosopher that is in the *GetFirstFork* state attempts to pick up the fork that is *to its right* if it is philosopher 1, otherwise it tries to pick up the fork that is *to its left*.  
   - The fork must be free. If it is, the philosopher becomes the owner of that fork and its program counter advances to *GetSecondFork*.  

2. **GetSecondFork**  
   - A philosopher that is in the *GetSecondFork* state now tries to pick up the opposite fork: the left fork for philosopher 1, otherwise the right fork.  
   - Again the fork must be free. If successful, the philosopher becomes the owner of that second fork and its program counter advances to *Eat*.  

3. **Eat**  
   - A philosopher in the *Eat* state may proceed only if it already owns **both** its left and right forks (the two forks it previously acquired).  
   - While eating the philosopher does not change the ownership of any fork; it simply moves its program counter forward to *ReleaseLeftFork*.  

4. **ReleaseLeftFork**  
   - A philosopher in the *ReleaseLeftFork* state puts down the fork that lies on its left side, making that fork free again.  
   - After releasing the left fork the philosopher’s program counter moves to *ReleaseRightFork*.  

5. **ReleaseRightFork**  
   - A philosopher in the *ReleaseRightFork* state puts down the fork that lies on its right side, again making it free.  
   - After releasing the right fork the philosopher returns to the initial step *GetFirstFork* and may start another dining cycle.  

**Fork‑Neighbour Relationships**

- The **right fork** of a given fork number *k* is *k + 1* unless *k* is the highest number, in which case the right fork is 1 (wrap‑around).  
- The **left fork** of a given fork number *k* is *k − 1* unless *k* equals 1, in which case the left fork is the highest fork number.  

These definitions ensure a circular table where each philosopher shares a fork with its two neighbours.

**Concurrency Model**

At each step the system may let **any** philosopher that satisfies the guard of an action perform that action. The actions are atomic: the change of fork ownership and the update of the program counter occur together. No philosopher can skip a step; it must follow the sequence *GetFirstFork → GetSecondFork → Eat → ReleaseLeftFork → ReleaseRightFork → GetFirstFork*.

**Safety Goal (Invariant)**

The specification contains a single invariant called *MutualExclusion*. It asserts that **no two different philosophers can be in the *Eat* state at the same time**. In other words, at any reachable configuration of the system, at most one philosopher is holding both of its forks and eating.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system guarantees that at any moment, at most one philosopher can be eating; that is, two distinct philosophers can never simultaneously be in the eating state while holding both of their required forks.

**System Overview**

The model describes a very small authentication protocol that mimics the core steps of Kerberos.  
There is a fixed collection of client identities, a single application server, and a single key‑distribution centre (KDC).  The protocol proceeds by exchanging messages over an unreliable network that may lose messages at any time.

**State variables**

* **clientState** – for each client the protocol records one of four local phases:  
  * *idle* – the client has not started a login.  
  * *wait_ticket* – the client has sent a request to the KDC and is waiting for a reply.  
  * *wait_auth* – the client has received a ticket from the KDC and has now sent an authentication request to the server, awaiting the server’s acknowledgement.  
  * *done* – the client has received the server’s acknowledgement and considers the authentication complete.

* **serverState** – for each client the server records either *idle* (no request has been accepted) or *accepted* (the server has accepted the client’s authentication).

* **kdcState** – the set of clients that have already been issued a ticket by the KDC.  A client appears in this set exactly when the KDC has processed that client’s request.

* **network** – the collection of messages that are currently “in flight”.  Messages are of four kinds: request from a client to the KDC, reply from the KDC containing a ticket, authentication request from a client to the server, and final acknowledgement from the server to the client.

* **replayCache** – the set of (client, nonce) pairs that the server has already processed.  It is used to detect and reject replayed authentication requests.

* **usedNonces** – the set of nonces that have already been generated by any client.  A client must choose a fresh nonce for each request.

**Protocol actions**

1. **Client sends a request** – A client that is idle may generate a fresh nonce, move its local state to *wait_ticket*, record the nonce as used, and place a request message (containing its identity and the nonce) onto the network.

2. **KDC replies** – When the KDC sees a request message on the network, it adds the client’s identity to *kdcState* (meaning the client now holds a ticket) and replaces the request with a reply message that carries the same nonce and a ticket that simply contains the client’s identity.  The client’s state and all other variables stay unchanged.

3. **Client forwards authentication** – A client that is waiting for a ticket may receive the KDC’s reply.  Upon receipt it changes its state to *wait_auth* and puts an authentication request onto the network.  This request contains the client’s identity, the original nonce, and the ticket received from the KDC.  The original reply message is removed from the network.

4. **Server accepts** – When the server reads an authentication request from the network, it checks three conditions: the ticket in the request must exactly match the client’s identity, the client must already be present in *kdcState* (i.e., the KDC must have issued a ticket), and the (client, nonce) pair must not already be in the replay cache.  If all checks succeed, the server records the client as *accepted*, adds the (client, nonce) pair to the replay cache, and sends an acknowledgement message back to the client.

5. **Server rejects** – If any of the three checks performed by the server fails (the ticket does not match the client, the client never received a ticket from the KDC, or the (client, nonce) pair has already been seen), the server simply discards the authentication request without changing any other state.

6. **Client receives acknowledgement** – A client that is waiting for authentication may receive the server’s acknowledgement.  It then moves its state to *done* and removes the acknowledgement from the network.

7. **Network loss** – At any moment any message that is currently in the network may be lost, in which case it is simply removed from the network collection.  No other state is affected.

**Safety guarantee**

The invariant that the model checks, called *AcceptRequiresTicket*, asserts that the server never marks a client as accepted unless that client has previously been recorded in the KDC’s ticket set.  In other words, the server’s acceptance decision is always based on a genuine ticket that was issued by the KDC.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
Whenever the server’s record shows a client as “accepted”, that client must already have been issued a ticket by the KDC; the server will never accept a client that has not previously received a valid ticket.

**System Overview**

The specification models a *bounded, multi‑node replicated ledger* that supports read‑write and read‑only transactions. The system is composed of a collection of nodes that maintain a common logical ledger, but each node can be in a different *view* (a configuration version). The model limits the number of view changes that can occur (the *view limit*) and the amount of history that can be stored (the *history limit*).  

---

### Core State Variables  

| Variable | Meaning (in plain English) |
|----------|----------------------------|
| **ledgerBranches** | A sequence that records the different *branches* (versions) of the ledger that have been created as the system changes view. Each branch contains the set of transactions that have been committed in that view. |
| **history** | A log of the observable events that the system has seen so far – for example, requests that have been sent, responses that have been received, and status queries. The log is kept only up to a fixed size (the *HistoryLimit*). |
| **Other variables** (inherited from the `MultiNode` and `MCSingleNode` modules) | Include the set of pending transaction requests, the set of transactions that have been committed, the set of transactions that have been marked invalid, and counters such as sequence numbers. They capture the normal operation of a replicated transaction processing system. |

---

### Actions (State Transitions)

1. **`MCTruncateLedgerAction`**  
   *Purpose*: Simulate a *view change* that discards old ledger branches.  
   *Guard*: The current number of ledger branches is strictly less than the configured *ViewLimit*. This guard ensures that the model never creates more branches than the allowed bound.  
   *Effect*: Executes the generic `TruncateLedgerAction` (defined in the single‑node module) which removes the oldest branch from `ledgerBranches`, thereby advancing the system to a new view while preserving the most recent state.

2. **`MCStatusInvalidResponseAction`**  
   *Purpose*: Model the handling of a *status‑invalid* response to a client that asks for the outcome of a transaction.  
   *Guard*: The length of the `history` log is below the configured *HistoryLimit*. This prevents the log from growing without bound.  
   *Effect*: Performs the generic `StatusInvalidResponseAction` (also defined in the single‑node module). The action records the receipt of an “invalid” status reply and updates the internal bookkeeping that the transaction is now known to be invalid.

3. **`MCNextSingleNodeAction`** (imported from `MCSingleNode`)  
   *Purpose*: Represents the ordinary work a node does when no view change or special status response is needed. This includes receiving transaction requests, executing them against the local ledger, committing them, and sending replies.  

4. **`MCNextMultiNodeAction`**  
   *Purpose*: The *overall* step that the system may take at any moment.  
   *Definition*: It is a nondeterministic choice among the three actions above: a normal single‑node step, a ledger‑truncation step, or a status‑invalid‑response step. In other words, at each logical time‑step the system may either process ordinary traffic, advance to a new view (subject to the view‑limit guard), or handle an invalid‑status reply (subject to the history‑limit guard).

5. **`MCSpecMultiNode`**  
   *Purpose*: Describes the complete execution of the system. It states that the system starts in an initial state (`Init`) and then repeatedly (forever) performs steps described by `MCNextMultiNodeAction`.  

---

### Safety Guarantees (Invariants)

The model declares a large collection of invariants that together express the *safety* of the replicated ledger. In everyday terms they guarantee:

* **Correct origin of observations** – every transaction that is observed as *received* was actually *sent* first.  
* **Commit observability** – a transaction can be observed as committed only after it has been sent and cannot later be observed as invalid.  
* **Request‑response consistency** – nodes only observe requests that they themselves have sent.  
* **Uniqueness** – transaction identifiers, request identifiers, and sequence numbers are all distinct; no two distinct transactions share the same identifier.  
* **Ordering** – committed read‑write transactions appear in the ledger in the same order as their logical sequence numbers, preserving a total order that respects real‑time order.  
* **Linearizability of reads** – read‑only transactions see a state of the ledger that could have resulted from some point‑in‑time ordering of the committed read‑write transactions; the system behaves as if all operations occurred atomically in a single global order.  
* **Strong consistency of status** – a transaction’s status is either *committed* or *invalid* and never both; once a transaction is committed, no later observation can claim it is invalid.  
* **At‑most‑once observation** – each transaction is observed at most once, preventing duplicate processing.  
* **Serializability of committed writes** – the set of committed read‑write transactions is serializable; their effects are equivalent to some serial execution that respects the observed order.

Because the model is *bounded* (the view limit is 3 and the history limit is 6), these guarantees are checked only within those finite bounds, but they are intended to hold for the unbounded system as well.

### Safety Property  

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** The system never reaches a state in which any of the listed invariants is violated; that is, throughout all executions, every transaction that is observed as committed was previously sent, transaction identifiers, requests and sequence numbers remain unique, committed transactions are ordered consistently with their sequence numbers, read‑only operations observe a linearizable view of the ledger, no transaction can be both committed and later reported as invalid, and each transaction is observed at most once. **System Overview** The model describes a kernel‑style read‑write lock (rw‑lock) that can be used by a set of concurrent threads. Each thread may act as a *reader*, a *writer*, or a *reader that later upgrades to a writer*. The lock supports the usual operations: * **shared (read) lock** – many threads may hold the lock simultaneously for reading. * **exclusive (write) lock** – only one thread may hold the lock for writing; no readers may be present. * **upgrade** – a thread that already holds a shared lock can attempt to convert its hold to an exclusive lock without releasing the lock first. * **downgrade** – a thread that holds an exclusive lock can release the write permission while retaining a shared lock. The model also captures the kernel’s wait‑queue mechanism that blocks threads when they cannot immediately acquire the lock and wakes them later when the lock becomes available. --- ### Main Variables | Variable | Meaning | |----------|---------| | **waitqs** | A table indexed by three *events* – **ReadEvent**, **WriteEvent**, **UpgradeEvent**. When the thread is later woken, it retries the acquisition loop. * **lck_rw_unlock_exclusive** – Releases an exclusive lock. It clears `x_locked`, `u_wanted`, and `r_count`. If no upgrade is pending and the lock is not held exclusively, it increments `r_count`. If after increment the lock is still not exclusive, the thread returns (the read critical section is entered). 3. If the lock is held exclusively or an upgrade is pending, the thread locks the **ReadEvent** queue, re‑examines the lock, and either (a) unlocks the queue and retries, or (b) records that there are shared waiters (`s_waiters := TRUE`) and blocks on the read queue. * **lck_rw_unlock_shared** – Decrements `r_count`. If after decrement the count becomes zero **and** either exclusive waiters (`x_waiters`) or an upgrade waiter (`u_waiter`) are present, it calls the wake‑up dispatcher to transfer the lock. #### 5. Upgrade (Shared → Exclusive) * **lck_rw_lock_shared_to_exclusive** – Implements the “upgrade” operation. 1. **Fast‑path**: if the thread is the *only* reader (`r_count = 1`) and no upgrade is already wanted, it atomically converts its shared hold to exclusive (`x_locked := TRUE`, `r_count := 0`) and reports success (`ret_try_u := TRUE`). 2. **Contended path**: otherwise, if no upgrade is currently wanted, the thread sets `u_wanted := TRUE` and enters the *upgrade* wait‑queue (`__lck_rw_lock_u2x_contended`). 3. Inside the contended path, the thread first releases its shared hold (`r_count := r_count – 1`). It then repeatedly checks whether the reader count has dropped to zero. If it does, it atomically acquires the exclusive lock and clears the upgrade flags. If not, it locks the **UpgradeEvent** queue, determines whether it must wait (because another upgrade waiter exists), records that it is waiting (`u_waiter := TRUE` if needed), and blocks. 4. If the upgrade fails (e.g., because the thread decided to give up), it releases the shared lock and returns `ret_try_u := FALSE`. * **lck_rw_unlock_exclusive** – (see above) also clears `u_wanted` after an upgrade completes, ensuring that no stale upgrade request remains. #### 6. Thread Behaviour (High‑level loops) Each thread repeatedly executes one of four behavioural loops, chosen nondeterministically at the start: * **Reader loop** – `rloop` → acquire shared lock (`lck_rw_lock_shared`) → execute critical section (`rcs`) → release shared lock (`lck_rw_unlock_shared`) → repeat. * **Upgrade loop** – `uloop` → acquire shared lock → critical section (`urcs`) → attempt upgrade (`lck_rw_lock_shared_to_exclusive`). If the upgrade succeeds, the thread executes an exclusive critical section (`uwcs`) and then releases the exclusive lock (`lck_rw_unlock_exclusive`). Regardless of success, the upgrade flag is cleared and the loop restarts. * **Writer loop** – `wloop` → acquire exclusive lock (`lck_rw_lock_exclusive`) → exclusive critical section (`wcs`) → release exclusive lock (`lck_rw_unlock_exclusive`) → repeat. * **Downgrade loop** – `dloop` → acquire exclusive lock → exclusive critical section (`dwcs`) → downgrade to shared (`lck_rw_lock_exclusive_to_shared`) → shared critical section (`drcs`) → release shared lock (`lck_rw_unlock_shared`) → repeat.
