When an urgent writer is waiting, the lock sets `x_urgent := TRUE` and gives those threads precedence during wake‑up. * **XBias** – Controls whether the lock prefers writers (`TRUE`) or readers (`FALSE`). In the wake‑up dispatcher, when `XBias = FALSE` the lock will first try to wake waiting readers (`lck_rw_wakeup_s`) before considering writers; when `XBias = TRUE` the writer‑wake‑up path is tried first. * **Threads** – The finite set of thread identifiers that the model checks; the invariant must hold for any permutation of this set (symmetry is expressed by the `Perms` definition). --- ### Safety Property (Invariant) The model includes the invariant named **Exclusion**. In plain English it guarantees: > **At any moment, if a thread is executing inside the exclusive (write) critical section, then no other thread can be executing in any critical section—neither a write nor a read.** Conversely, if any thread is inside a read critical section, no thread can be inside a write critical section at the same time. This property enforces the fundamental mutual‑exclusion contract of a read‑write lock: writers obtain exclusive access, and readers are allowed to proceed concurrently only when no writer holds the lock. **SAFETY PROPERTY:** Only one thread may be inside the write critical section at a time, and while a thread holds the write lock no other thread may be inside either a read or a write critical section. Consequently, the lock never permits a writer and a reader (or two writers) to be in their respective critical sections simultaneously.

**System Overview**

The model describes a classic river‑crossing puzzle involving four participants: a farmer, a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage.  
All participants start on the *starting bank* of a river; the opposite bank is called the *ending bank*.  

Two state variables keep track of the current location of each participant:

* **Start** – the set of participants that are currently on the starting bank.  
* **End** – the set of participants that are currently on the ending bank.  

At any moment each participant belongs to exactly one of these two sets.

**Initial Situation**

At the beginning of the execution all four participants are on the starting bank and the ending bank is empty.

**Allowed Moves**

The only way the system can evolve is by the farmer piloting a small boat that can carry the farmer plus at most one additional item. Two kinds of moves are possible:

1. **Cross to the ending bank**  
   *Precondition*: the farmer is on the starting bank.  
   *Action*: the farmer selects one item that is also on the starting bank (the item may be the wolf, the goat, the cabbage, or none – the model forces the selection of exactly one item). The farmer and the chosen item are removed from the starting bank and placed on the ending bank.  

2. **Return to the starting bank**  
   *Precondition*: the farmer is on the ending bank.  
   *Action*: the farmer selects one item that is on the ending bank. The farmer and the chosen item are removed from the ending bank and placed back on the starting bank.  

After every move the model checks the safety of both banks:

* If the farmer is not present on a bank, that bank must **not** contain both the wolf and the goat together, because the wolf would eat the goat.  
* Likewise, if the farmer is absent, the bank must **not** contain both the goat and the cabbage together, because the goat would eat the cabbage.

These checks are performed for both the starting bank and the ending bank after each crossing, ensuring that no forbidden pairing is left unattended.

**System Evolution**

The system repeatedly performs either a crossing to the ending bank or a return crossing to the starting bank, indefinitely, as long as the pre‑conditions and safety checks are satisfied.

**Safety Guarantees (Invariants)**

The model enforces three invariants throughout execution:

1. **Never all items on the ending bank** – the set of participants on the ending bank is never equal to the full collection of farmer, wolf, goat, and cabbage.  
2. **Goat never left alone with cabbage** – on any bank, if the goat and the cabbage are together, the farmer must also be present on that same bank.  
3. **Wolf never left alone with goat** – on any bank, if the wolf and the goat are together, the farmer must also be present on that same bank.

These invariants together constitute the safety property that the system must maintain.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At no time may the wolf and goat be left together without the farmer, nor may the goat and cabbage be left together without the farmer, and the collection of all four participants never simultaneously resides on the ending bank.

**System Overview**

The specification models a library that manages a single logical *instance* and provides a set of API functions that can be called by a client program. Each call may succeed or return one of several predefined error codes. The model captures the internal state of the library, the conditions under which a call is made, and the deterministic rule that decides which error code (if any) is returned.

---

### State Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **instance** | Indicates whether an instance currently exists. It can be either *NONE* (no instance) or *CREATED* (an instance has been successfully created). |
| **preInstance** | Stores the value of **instance** *just before* the most recent API call. It is used to evaluate the error that was returned for that call. |
| **lastOp** | The name of the API operation that was executed most recently (e.g., *CREATE*, *STEP*, *GET_VERSION*). The special value *NONE* means that no operation has been performed yet. |
| **lastError** | The error code that was returned by the most recent operation. The set of possible codes includes “OK”, “NULL_HANDLE”, “REENTRANT_CALL”, “WRONG_THREAD”, and several others that represent specific failure modes. |
| **threadState** | Records whether the thread that issued the last call is the *owner* of the instance (*OWNER*) or some other thread (*OTHER*). |
| **configState** | Represents the validity of the configuration supplied to the call. It can be *VALID*, *INVALID*, or *WRONG_VER* (wrong version). |
| **bufferState** | Indicates whether the buffer supplied to the call is large enough (*SUFFICIENT*) or too small (*TOO_SMALL*). |
| **reentState** | Tracks whether the library is already inside a *STEP* operation (*IN_STEP*) or not (*CLEAR*). This is used to detect re‑entrant calls to *STEP*. |
| **opCount** | Counts how many API calls have been performed so far. It is bounded by a configurable constant **MaxOps**. |

---

### Initialization

When the system starts, there is no instance (`instance = NONE`), no previous operation (`lastOp = NONE`), and the library is in a clean state: the calling thread is the owner, the configuration is valid, the buffer is sufficient, and no re‑entrancy flag is set. The operation counter is zero and the initial error code is “OK”.

---

### API Call Execution (the **ExecuteOp** action)

An API call is modeled by the **ExecuteOp** action, which proceeds as follows:

1. **Pre‑condition Check** – The action can only be taken while the number of performed calls is less than **MaxOps**.
2. **Snapshot of Current State** – The current instance state is saved into **preInstance**; the supplied thread, configuration, buffer, and re‑entrancy flags become the new values of **threadState**, **configState**, **bufferState**, and **reentState**.
3. **Operation Recording** – The name of the invoked operation is stored in **lastOp**.
4. **Error Determination** – The model calls a deterministic function (the *error resolution function*) that examines the operation name together with the snapshot of all pre‑conditions (instance state, thread state, configuration state, buffer state, re‑entrancy state) and returns the appropriate error code according to a fixed priority order:
   * *GET_VERSION* always succeeds.
   * *CREATE* checks whether an instance already exists, whether the configuration is invalid, and whether the version is mismatched, in that order.
   * *DESTROY* treats a null handle (no instance) as a no‑op, otherwise it checks that the calling thread is the owner.
   * Core operations (*STEP*, *RESET*, *CAPTURE_TEXT*, *CAPTURE_RGB*, *KEY_EVENT*, *MOUSE_EVENT*, *SAVE_STATE*, *LOAD_STATE*, *STATE_HASH*) are checked in the following priority: null handle → wrong thread → re‑entrant call (only for *STEP*) → buffer too small (only for operations that need a buffer) → success.
   * Any operation not listed falls through to an “INTERNAL” error.
5. **Result Storage** – The error code produced by the resolution function is stored in **lastError**.
6. **Instance State Update** – If the call was *CREATE* and succeeded, **instance** becomes *CREATED*. If the call was *DESTROY* and succeeded while an instance existed, **instance** becomes *NONE*. All other operations leave the instance state unchanged.
7. **Operation Counter** – **opCount** is incremented.

The **Next** relation allows the system to either perform another **ExecuteOp** with any combination of the pre‑condition values, or to remain unchanged (a stutter step). This nondeterministic choice explores all possible sequences of API calls and environmental conditions.

---

### Deterministic Error Logic (the “ResolveError” function)

The error logic is a pure, deterministic mapping from the tuple *(operation, instance state, thread state, configuration state, buffer state, re‑entrancy state)* to a single error code. The priority order guarantees that when several error conditions are simultaneously true, the one that appears first in the list is the one returned. This mirrors the guard‑clause checks in the reference C implementation.

---

### Safety Invariants (the properties that must always hold)

The model asserts several invariants that capture the intended safety guarantees of the library:

* **Deterministic Error Codes** – For every operation that has been performed, the stored error code exactly matches the result of the deterministic error resolution function applied to the pre‑conditions of that operation.
* **Success Requires a Valid Instance** – Whenever a core operation reports “OK”, the library must have been in the *CREATED* state before the call.
* **Error Codes Are Valid** – Every error value stored in **lastError** belongs to the predefined set of 15 error codes.
* **Null‑Handle Consistency** – The “NULL_HANDLE” error appears only when a core operation is attempted while no instance exists.
* **Re‑entrancy Detection** – The “REENTRANT_CALL” error appears only when a *STEP* operation is issued while the library is already inside a *STEP* (the re‑entrancy flag is *IN_STEP*).
* **Wrong‑Thread Detection** – The “WRONG_THREAD” error appears only when the calling thread is not the owner of the instance.

All of these invariants are checked after each transition, ensuring that no execution can violate the specified safety constraints.

---

### Behavioural Summary

In plain terms, the model describes a simple resource manager that:

* Allows a client to create and destroy a singleton resource.
* Provides a suite of operations that can only be used while the resource exists and only by the owning thread.
* Returns precise, deterministic error codes that reflect the exact reason for failure, following a well‑defined priority.
* Detects and prevents illegal re‑entrant calls to the *STEP* operation.
* Guarantees that successful core operations are only possible when the resource has been properly created.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system guarantees that every API call returns exactly the error code prescribed by the deterministic error‑resolution rules, and that each error code can occur only under its specific pre‑condition (e.g., “NULL_HANDLE” only when no instance exists, “WRONG_THREAD” only when called from a non‑owner thread, “REENTRANT_CALL” only when a step is invoked while already in a step). Consequently, successful core operations are possible only when an instance is created, and no illegal or unexpected error codes can be produced.

**System Overview**  
The model represents a tiny lifecycle manager for a single logical component (the *instance*) that can be created, stepped through a protected operation, and destroyed. The manager is accessed through a small set of API calls that can be invoked from two possible threads – a *Main* thread and an *Other* thread. The model limits the total number of API calls to a small constant (six) so that the state‑space stays tiny for exhaustive model checking.

---

### Variables (state kept by the manager)

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **instance** | The lifecycle state of the component. It is either **NONE** (the component does not exist) or **CREATED** (the component has been successfully created). |
| **handle** | A token that represents a reference to the component. It is **NULL** when the component does not exist and **VALID** when the component has been created. |
| **opCount** | A counter of how many API calls have been performed so far. It is bounded by the constant *MaxOperations* (set to 6 in the configuration). |
| **lastError** | The error code returned by the most recent API call. Possible values are **OK**, **NULL_HANDLE**, **ALREADY_CREATED**, **INVALID_CONFIG**, **VERSION_MISMATCH**, **REENTRANT_CALL**, and **WRONG_THREAD**. |
| **ownerThread** | The identifier of the thread that created the component. It is either **Main**, **Other**, or the special value **None** when no component exists. |
| **currentThread** | The identifier of the thread that is executing the next API call. It can be **Main** or **Other** and may be changed by a thread‑switch action. |
| **inStep** | A Boolean flag that is true while a *step* operation is in progress. It is used to detect re‑entrant calls to the step routine. |

---

### Actions (API calls)

1. **CreateOK** – *legends_create* with a valid configuration.  
   *Preconditions*: the component does not exist and the operation limit has not been reached.  
   *Effect*: the component becomes **CREATED**, a **VALID** handle is issued, the calling thread becomes the owner, the error code is set to **OK**, and the operation counter is incremented.

2. **CreateAlready** – *legends_create* when the component is already created.  
   *Preconditions*: the component is **CREATED** and the operation limit has not been reached.  
   *Effect*: the state does not change, the error code becomes **ALREADY_CREATED**, and the operation counter is incremented.

3. **CreateBadConfig** – *legends_create* with an invalid configuration.  
   *Preconditions*: the component is **NONE** and the operation limit has not been reached.  
   *Effect*: the component stays absent, the error code becomes **INVALID_CONFIG**, and the operation counter is incremented.

4. **CreateBadVersion** – *legends_create* when the supplied version does not match.  
   *Preconditions*: same as the previous action.  
   *Effect*: the component stays absent, the error code becomes **VERSION_MISMATCH**, and the operation counter is incremented.

5. **Destroy** – *legends_destroy*.  
   *Preconditions*: operation limit not exceeded.  
   *Effect*:  
   * If there is no valid handle (**NULL**), the call succeeds silently (error **OK**) and nothing changes.  
   * If the caller is not the owning thread, the call fails with **WRONG_THREAD** and nothing changes.  
   * Otherwise, the component is torn down: state returns to **NONE**, handle becomes **NULL**, owner is cleared, the re‑entrancy flag is cleared, and the error code is **OK**.  
   In every case the operation counter is incremented.

6. **Step** – a protected *legends_step_* operation that may be called repeatedly while the component exists.  
   *Preconditions*: operation limit not exceeded.  
   *Effect*:  
   * If there is no valid handle, the call fails with **NULL_HANDLE**.  
   * If the caller is not the owner, the call fails with **WRONG_THREAD**.  
   * If a step is already in progress (`inStep` is true), the call fails with **REENTRANT_CALL**.  
   * Otherwise the step starts successfully: the error code becomes **OK** and `inStep` is set to true.  
   The operation counter is incremented.

7. **StepDone** – marks the end of a previously started step.  
   *Preconditions*: `inStep` is true.  
   *Effect*: clears the re‑entrancy flag (sets `inStep` to false) without changing any other state. The operation counter is unchanged.

8. **CoreAPI** – a generic placeholder for other core API calls such as *CAPTURE*, *INPUT*, *SAVE*, *LOAD*.  
   *Preconditions*: operation limit not exceeded.  
   *Effect*:  
   * Returns **NULL_HANDLE** if there is no valid handle.  
   * Returns **WRONG_THREAD** if the caller is not the owner.  
   * Otherwise returns **OK**.  
   No other state is modified; the operation counter is incremented.

9. **SwitchThread** – simulates a context switch between the two threads.  
   *Effect*: toggles `currentThread` between **Main** and **Other**; all other variables stay unchanged.

10. **No‑op (UNCHANGED)** – the model also allows a step in which none of the above actions occur, leaving the whole state unchanged.

---

### Safety Guarantees (the invariant)

The model includes a collection of safety invariants that must hold in every reachable state:

* **At most one active instance** – whenever the component is marked as **CREATED**, the handle is guaranteed to be **VALID**; the model never allows two independent instances to coexist.  
* **Misuse returns an error code, not a crash** – if the component does not exist and the handle is **NULL**, any API call will set `lastError` to one of the defined error codes (including **OK** for harmless calls) instead of causing an undefined state.  
* **Handle consistency** – the handle being **NULL** is exactly equivalent to the component being absent (**NONE**); the two variables are always in sync.  
* **Re‑entrancy guard** – while a step is in progress (`inStep` = true), any further call to the step routine is rejected with the error **REENTRANT_CALL**; successful step calls can only occur when `inStep` is false.  
* **Wrong‑thread protection** – when a component exists, only the thread that created it (the *owner*) may receive an **OK** result from core API calls; any other thread gets the error **WRONG_THREAD**.  
* **Configuration validation** – if a creation attempt fails because the configuration is invalid, the component remains absent; an invalid configuration can never cause the component to be created.

Together, these conditions ensure that the lifecycle manager behaves predictably: resources are never duplicated, error handling is deterministic, thread ownership is respected, and re‑entrant use of the step routine is prevented.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** The system guarantees that at any moment there is at most one created instance with a matching valid handle, that the handle and instance state are always consistent, that any misuse of the API (null handle, wrong thread, re‑entrant step, or invalid configuration) results in a well‑defined error code rather than an undefined or crashed state, and that only the owning thread can successfully invoke core operations while a step is in progress cannot be entered again until it is completed.

The model describes a small image‑loading service that works with a fixed number of images (three in the given configuration). Each image progresses through a lifecycle that is managed by a queue and by a pool of cryptographic keys that must be generated in batches before the images can be marked as ready.

| Variable | Meaning |

| **image_states** | A mapping that records, for every image, which of the four possible states it is currently in: *None* (not yet requested), *PendingKey* (a load has been requested but a key is still missing), *HasKey* (a key has been assigned but loading is not finished), or *Loaded* (the image has been fully loaded). |
| **image_queue** | An ordered list (a FIFO queue) that contains the identifiers of images that have been started but not yet finished. The head of the list is the image that is currently at the front of the processing pipeline. |
| **keys_used** | A counter that records how many keys have been handed out so far. |
| **keys** | An ordered list that holds the keys that have already been generated but not yet assigned to an image. Each element of the list is simply the token “Generated”. |
| **keys_batch** | A Boolean flag that indicates whether a batch of keys has been generated and is waiting to be consumed. When true, the list *keys* contains at least one generated key. |
| **pending_keys** | A mapping from each worker thread to the number of keys that the thread is currently responsible for generating. A value of zero means the thread is idle; a positive value means the thread is in the middle of a batch generation. |
| **Thread** | The set of identifiers for the worker threads that can generate keys. In the concrete instance there are three threads, numbered 1, 2 and 3. |
| **Image** | The set of image identifiers, also three in the concrete instance, numbered 1, 2 and 3. |
| **ImageState** | The enumeration of the four possible states listed above. |

---

### Actions (State Transitions)

1. **Initialisation**  
   All images start in the *None* state, the queue is empty, no keys have been generated, the batch flag is false, the key‑usage counter is zero, and every thread is idle (its pending‑keys count is zero).

2. **StartLoad(i)** – *request to load an image*  
   When an image *i* is still in the *None* state, the system may start loading it. The image’s state changes to *PendingKey* and the image identifier is appended to the end of the queue. No other variable changes.

3. **StartKeyGeneration(t)** – *begin a batch of key creation*  
   A thread *t* may start a batch only if every thread currently has zero pending work. The thread looks at how many images are waiting for a key (the number of images whose state is *PendingKey*) and computes how many additional keys are needed to match that number. That amount is recorded in the thread’s entry of *pending_keys*, and the batch flag is set to true. No keys are actually generated yet.

4. **GenerateKeys(t)** – *produce the batch*  
   If thread *t* has a positive pending‑keys count, it creates exactly that many “Generated” tokens, concatenates them to the end of the *keys* list, and then resets its pending‑keys count to zero. The batch flag remains true.

5. **SetKey(i)** – *assign a generated key to the front image*  
   This action can fire only when there is at least one generated key waiting, the batch flag is true, and the image at the head of the queue is *i* (the same image that is currently in *PendingKey*). The first key is removed from the *keys* list, the image’s state changes from *PendingKey* to *HasKey*, and the key‑usage counter is incremented. The queue and other variables stay unchanged.

6. **FinishLoad(i)** – *complete loading of an image that already has a key*  
   When the front image *i* is in the *HasKey* state, the system may finish its loading. The image’s state becomes *Loaded*. No other variable changes.

7. **DequeImage(i)** – *remove a loaded image from the queue*  
   If the front of the queue is an image *i* that is already *Loaded*, the head element is removed from the queue, and the batch flag is cleared (set to false). All other variables stay the same.

8. **Done** – *terminal condition*  
   The system is considered finished when every image has reached the *Loaded* state. At that point no further state changes occur.

9. **Next** – *overall step*  
   The system repeatedly chooses any enabled action among the ones above (including the *Done* condition). In addition, any thread may independently start a key‑generation batch or actually generate its pending batch.

---

### Intended Behaviour

- Images are loaded in the order they are requested.  
- A key must be generated for each image before the loading can be completed.  
- Keys are produced in batches: a thread first declares how many keys it will generate, then creates exactly that many in one atomic step.  
- The batch flag guarantees that generated keys are only consumed while the corresponding batch is still “open”.  
- Once an image has been loaded and removed from the queue, the system may start another batch if more images are still pending.

---

### Safety Property (Invariant)

The model enforces two invariants:

1. **Type correctness** – All variables always hold values of the expected kind (the queue is a sequence of image identifiers, the state map always maps every image to one of the four allowed states, etc.).  

2. **Key‑to‑image balance** – Whenever there is at least one generated key waiting in the *keys* list, the total number of generated keys never exceeds the number of images that are currently awaiting a key (i.e., images whose state is *PendingKey*). In other words, the system never creates more keys than there are images that need them.

These invariants together guarantee that the system cannot lose track of keys or assign keys to images that are not expecting them, and that the queue and state machine remain consistent throughout execution.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At every reachable state, if the list of generated keys is non‑empty then the count of those keys is never greater than the number of images that are still in the “PendingKey” state; thus the system always maintains a one‑to‑one correspondence between waiting images and available keys.

**System Overview**

The model describes a tiny asynchronous lock manager that coordinates a fixed set of tasks (for the concrete configuration the tasks are *Task1*, *Task2* and *Task3*).  
The manager keeps track of three pieces of information:

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **taskStates** | A mapping that records, for each task, which logical phase it is currently in. The possible phases are **running**, **acquired**, **waiting**, **wakeup**, **canceled** and **done**. |
| **lockState** | A single flag that tells whether the lock is **locked** (some task currently owns it) or **unlocked** (no owner). |
| **waiters** | An ordered list (a FIFO queue) of the tasks that have tried to acquire the lock but could not because it was already held. The head of the list is the task that will be given the lock next when it becomes available. |

The system starts with an initialization step (provided by the `step1` module) that puts every task into the **running** state, sets the lock to **unlocked**, and makes the *waiters* list empty.

---

### Actions

All state changes are expressed as *actions* that may be executed by any task. The model’s overall step (`Next`) nondeterministically picks a task and lets it perform one of the following actions:

1. **Acquire(task)** – *Attempt to take the lock*  
   *Pre‑condition*:  
   – No task is currently in the **wakeup** state (the model forbids a new acquisition while a previously woken task is pending).  
   – The invoking task is currently **running**.  

   *Behaviour*:  
   – **If the lock is free** (`lockState = unlocked`) **and** every task that is already in the *waiters* queue has been marked **canceled**, the lock can be handed to the requesting task immediately: the task’s state becomes **acquired**, the lock flag switches to **locked**, and the *waiters* list is left unchanged.  
   – **Otherwise** (the lock is already held, or there are non‑canceled tasks waiting), the requesting task cannot obtain the lock now: its state is changed to **waiting** and it is appended to the end of the *waiters* queue. The lock flag stays as it was.

2. **Cancel(task)** – *Give up the attempt* (definition lives in the `step2` module)  
   When a task decides it no longer wants the lock, its state is changed from **waiting** (or **running**) to **canceled**. The task remains in the *waiters* queue, but the cancelation later allows other tasks to bypass it.

3. **Release(task)** – *Return the lock* (definition lives in `step1`)  
   The task that currently holds the lock (its state is **acquired**) can release it. The lock flag is set back to **unlocked** and the releasing task’s state becomes **running** again. If there are waiting tasks that have not been canceled, the release action may also trigger a wake‑up (see below).

4. **WakeUp(task)** – *Prepare the next waiting task* (definition lives in `step1`)  
   The first non‑canceled task in the *waiters* queue is moved from **waiting** to **wakeup**. This marks the task as the one that will be allowed to acquire the lock on its next attempt, preventing any other task from jumping ahead.

5. **Finished(task)** – *Terminate a task* (definition lives in `step1`)  
   When a task has completed all its work, its state is changed to **done**. After this point the task no longer participates in lock acquisition or release.

All actions preserve the overall set of tasks; they only change the values of the three variables described above.

---

### Intended Behaviour

* A task that is **running** may try to acquire the lock.  
* If the lock is free and no other waiting task is still active, the task becomes **acquired** and the lock becomes **locked** – exclusive ownership.  
* If the lock is not free, the task joins the *waiters* queue and becomes **waiting**.  
* A waiting task may be **canceled**, removing its claim to the lock while leaving its place in the queue (so that later logic can skip it).  
* When the current owner releases the lock, the first non‑canceled waiting task is **woken up**; it will be the only task allowed to acquire the lock next.  
* Once a task finishes its work it enters the **done** state and no longer affects the lock.

The queue ensures FIFO ordering among non‑canceled waiters, and the *wakeup* guard guarantees that at most one waiting task is in the privileged “next‑in‑line” position at any moment.

---

### Safety Property

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At all times, no more than one task can be in the **acquired** state; that is, the lock is never held simultaneously by two different tasks. This invariant guarantees mutual exclusion for the critical section protected by the lock.
